newsitem.title: CHINA: Danish pork industry seen having choice of markets.
newsitem.headline: Danish pork industry seen having choice of markets.

text.p: The major beneficiary of the current outbreak of hog disease in Europe is likely to be Denmark, which now has a choice of markets for its pork products, a senior U.S. industry official said on Thursday.

The outbreak in the Netherlands of swine fever, coupled with the foot and mouth crisis in Taiwan, gives Denmark a choice of Europe and Japan, Joel Haggard, Asia Pacific regional vice-president of the U.S. Meat Export Federation said.
Dutch television reported on Wednesday that the country's Farm Ministry was planning to cull around a million pigs at 1,600 farms to snuff out a swine fever epidemic in the south.
It said that so far some 650,000 pigs had been destroyed in an attempt to contain the highly contagious disease.

China on Wednesday announced a ban on the import of pork and beef from the Netherlands, as well as pork from Germany, because of fears of hog cholera and mad cow disease, the official Xinhua news agency said.
The ban covered imports of German and Dutch pork and pork products and prohibited the posting or carrying of such items into China, Xinhua said.
Dutch cows, cow embryos, beef, beef products and animal feed made from ground cow bones and other livestock would be banned as well, the agency said.
The measures were being taken to protect Chinese livestock from possible contamination from hog cholera, which had broken out in Germany in January and in the Netherlands in February, it said.
Sources in Beijing and Hong Kong said China is self-sufficient in pork production, though it does import some non-muscle variety meats.
The Netherlands is a major supplier of live hogs to Europe, but accounted for only 2,624 tonnes of 60,110 tonnes of live hogs imported by Hong Kong in 1996, Haggard told Reuters.
However, the Netherlands was the second largest supplier of variety meats, or offal products, to Hong Kong, he said, providing 25,176 tonnes of a total in 1996 of 105,838 tonnes.
Most of Hong Kong's variety meat imports were re-exported to China, he said.
"So unless restrictions are placed on Hong Kong's imports of these products, they are mostly going to China," he said.
Hong Kong's government is yet to announce any ban on the import of Dutch pork variety meats.

Denmark now faced a choice, Haggard said, of making up the shortfall in Europe, or of sending its pork to Japan to fill the void left there by Taiwan's withdrawal from that market after the recent outbreak in Taiwan of hog foot and mouth disease.

Swine exports from the Netherlands to Germany in 1996 totalled three million head, to Spain 1.2 million head, to Italy one million head, to Belgium 850,000 head and to France 500,000 head, figures provided by the federation show.
Sources in the region said China would be unlikely to pick up any slack in regional pork supply as the country was not considered free of hog foot and mouth disease.
